<reason>Both sides argued the real motion competently, and the debate narrowed cleanly to one clash: a fixed five-year completion deadline versus CON's conditional "demonstrated delivery" trigger. CON conceded the regressivity arithmetic and built its route on exclusion error and indirect pass-through (the unregistered worker who loses cheap fares and food transport but never appears on a registry). That point stayed alive, and CON deserves credit for answering PRO's Q1 with an actual specifiable threshold rather than dodging. But PRO won the two comparisons that decided the round. First, the symmetry turn: CON invented a demanding audit (95% coverage, timely payment, 30-day appeals, independent surveys) and aimed it only at the reform, while the instrument it protects would fail that same test outright and has no recipients or appeals at all — and the audit itself presupposes exactly the administrative capacity CON says fragile states lack, so the veto bites hardest where the regressive transfer and smuggling are worst. CON's closing answered this only with status-quo-bias assertion ("withdrawing an existing cushion requires proof"), never explaining why the burden is asymmetric. Second, PRO's crisis reframe — an uncapped price-driven subsidy is the line that gets slashed overnight in a fiscal shock, whereas a cash transfer with named recipients is politically defended — reversed CON's risk story, and CON's reply (cash may lose purchasing power) did not neutralize it. PRO also handled its own pressure honestly by ordering claims on savings (protection first, public services residual), accepting a real cost rather than dodging. Deductions to PRO for a nonexistent reference id and for asserting silence on Q2 that chronology had not yet permitted CON to answer; deductions to CON for leaving the political-economy point ("without a date, 'not yet' becomes permanent") largely unrebutted.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's closing turn of CON's own audit standard back on the subsidy: applying the 95%-coverage, timely-payment, 30-day-appeals test to the instrument CON defends shows it fails on its face, and the test demands precisely the state capacity CON claims is missing — leaving CON with an asymmetric burden it never justified.</best_rebuttal>
